## Abstract

Large-scale CO2 injection for geo-sequestration in deep saline aquifers can significantly increase 
reservoir pressure, which, if not appropriately managed, can lead to potential environmental risk. Brine 
extraction from the aquifer has been proposed as a method to control the reservoir pressure and increase 
storage capacity. However, iterative optimization of the well controls for this scenario using highresolution dynamic simulation models can be computationally expensive.

$$
\mathrm{CO}_{2}
$$

In this paper, we demonstrate the application of a so-called coarse–grid network model (CGNet) as a 
reduced-order model for efficient simulation and optimization of CO2 sequestration with brine extraction. 
As a proxy, CGNet is configured by aggressively coarsening the fine-scale grid and then tuning the 
parameters of the associated simulation graph (transmissibility, pore volumes, well indices, and relative 
permeability endpoints) by minimizing the mismatch of well-response data (rates, bottom-hole pressure) 
and saturation distribution from the fine-scale model. Calibration and optimization procedures are 
automated using gradient-based optimization methods that leverage automatic differentiation capabilities 
in the reservoir simulator in the same way backpropagation methods are used in training neural networks. 
Once calibrated, CGNet is employed for well-control optimization. Validation with the fine-scale model 
shows that CGNet closely matches the optimized net-present value (NPV). Numerical examples using the 
Johansen model, available as a public dataset, shows that the optimization can be accelerated up to seven 
times using CGNet compared with a fine-scale model. (Using a compiled language will likely result in 
significantly larger speedups as small models suffer from a disproportionately high computational 
overhead when executed in MATLAB.)  This study implies that a reduced-order model such as CGNet 
can be a powerful data-driven tool for faster evaluation of CO2 geo-sequestration simulation, combined
with proper reservoir monitoring program.

## Introduction

Geological CO2 sequestration is a critical solution to significantly reduce CO2 emission from large 
stationary sources (Bui et al., 2018; Metz et al., 2005). It has been proven to be a viable technology for 
long-term storage of CO2 through utilization of  the various trapping mechanism that can take place in 
subsurface porous media such as deep saline aquifer (Krevor et al., 2023). However, injecting CO2 at large 
scale can significantly increase aquifer pressure. If this pressure exceeds the formation breakdown 
pressure, it can potentially compromise caprock integrity and open leakage pathways (Orr, 2018). This 
can limit the practical storage capacity for industrial-scale implementation of CO2 sequestration.

To alleviate this issue, brine extraction from the aquifer has been proposed as an alternative for pressure 
management strategy (Bergmo et al., 2011; Birkholzer et al., 2012). Although it has potential to increase 
CO2 storage capacity, brine extraction scheme can introduce additional investment which can challenge 
economic feasibility of a sequestration project (Sullivan et al., 2013). Therefore, minimizing the volume 
of extracted brine, while maximizing stored CO2 and meeting other techno-economic constraints, is vital
for a safe and efficient CO2 sequestration project.

Optimization of the pressure management scenarios for this problem commonly involves the usage of 
large-scale high-fidelity dynamic flow simulation, which requires a well-characterized geological model 
as an input. Implementing this approach in iterative optimization methods can be prohibitive due to the 
substantial computational cost involved in running the forward simulations. Moreover, deep saline 
aquifers are typically less characterized compared to petroleum reservoirs, which can impose extra effort 
of uncertainty quantification for the geological model.

These considerations motivate the use of data-driven models for pressure management. Numerous datadriven models aiming to optimize brine extraction in CO2 sequestration have been proposed that leverage 
machine learning (ML) techniques like neural networks (Musayev et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2021; Yan et 
al., 2022a, 2022c) and semi-analytic approaches such as the capacitance-resistance model (Tao and 
Bryant, 2015). These models can be trained using observed data from wells and 4D seismic monitoring,
or trained on simulation data from high-resolution numerical simulator to be used as a proxy model (Chen 
et al., 2023; Tariq et al., 2023). Once these models achieve sufficient training accuracy, they can be 
employed for rapid optimization, as their computational cost is significantly lower compared to traditional 
numerical simulations.

Although ML-based models exhibit the capability to predict physical states near their training data, 
they may yield non-physical predictions if not subjected to physics constraints during the training process. 
Consequently, the reliability of these models to generalize beyond the training data diminishes. To resolve 
this issue, physics-informed machine learning has been developed by incorporating governing partial 
differential equations (PDE) as a residual term in the cost function for model training (Shokouhi et al., 
2021; Yan et al., 2022b). This approach has significantly enhanced the accuracy of ML methods even
when trained on a limited dataset. Nevertheless, interpreting ML models in a physical sense remains a 
challenging task.

Numerical flow network models have gained increasing popularity as reliable physics-based datadriven models for reservoir management (Ren et al., 2023). In essence, flow network models provide 
simplified flow connection between wells and reservoir nodes through semi-analytic flow equations (Guo 
et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2015) or through a series of 1D standard finite-volume grids with specific interwell connection rules (Lerlertpakdee et al., 2014; Lutidze, 2018; Ren et al., 2019). These types of models 
have shown decent results for simulating various complex flow physics, including two phase flow in 
heterogeneous diatomite reservoir (Wang et al., 2021) and oil recovery from steam-flooding (Wang et al., 
2022).

In this paper, we investigate CGNet (Lie and Krogstad, 2022), an alternative numerical flow network, 
as a viable approach for developing physics-based reduced-order models in CO2 sequestration. CGNet 
differs from other flow network model, as it provides richer networks with more tunable parameters per 
grid cells and a larger set of inherent network path, which makes it more robust to calibrate (Lie and

Krogstad, 2023). In its simplest form, a CGNet can be derived from a standard 3D structured mesh (either 
rectilinear or curvilinear) that provides a rough representation of the storage medium's structural outline. 
Reservoir and well node parameters in the resulting finite-volume simulation graph are then calibrated to 
minimize the mismatch with observed well data such as rates and bottom-hole pressure. Like other datadriven model paradigms such as GPSNet or StellNet, calibrating well and petro-physical parameters in 
CGNet does not necessarily preserve the reservoir's local characteristics or geological features, even 
though physically reasonable limits can be imposed on these parameters. This approach can nonetheless
be very useful if a well characterized geological model is not available, or too complex to calibrate.

This study aims to extend the application of CGNet as a reduced-order model for optimizing well 
controls in geological CO2 sequestration with brine extraction. We implemented our CGNet models using
a fully differentiable open-source reservoir simulation platform, MRST 2022a (Lie, 2019). Our calibration 
and optimization procedures rely on gradient-based, adjoint optimization methods, such as Gauss-Newton 
or Quasi-Netwton, that leverage the automatic differentiation capabilities in MRST in the same way 
backpropagation methods are used in training neural networks. Numerical examples are derived from a 
public dataset modelling a prospective injection in the Johansen aquifer (Eigestad et al., 2009)  as an 
example of realistic deep saline aquifer settings. The model stems from an early study of the area that was 
later developed as the Northern Lights storage facility.

This paper is structured as the following. We first illustrate the model equations and configurations of 
the CGNet; then we describe how to calibrate the CGNet to the fine-scale model output. We also discuss 
how the calibration results are affected by different CGNet configurations and tuning parameters. We then 
discuss the well control optimization from the calibrated CGNet and the subsequent validation in the finescale reference model.

## Model Training

In this section, we investigate how well CGNet reproduces and predicts synthetic well responses taken 
from a numerical simulation of a realistic fine-scale geological aquifer model. For this case study, we use 
a sector model of Johansen formation, available as a public dataset from the MatMoRa project website
(https://www.sintef.no/projectweb/matmora/). The Johansen formation is located offshore the southwestern coast of Norway and contains the storage site for the large-scale Northern Lights project. The 
sector model used herein comes from an early-phase study of the formation and describes a scenario with 
a planned capacity on the order of 4 Mt CO2/year (Eigestad et al., 2009). The geometry of the sector model 
is described as 100 ×100 × 1 corner point grids with 6,559 active cells and has several major faults. The 
permeability of the Johansen formation is fairly high, ranging from 64 to 1660 mD. **Figure** 2a shows the 
permeability distribution of the sector models used as reference. The fluid properties for CO2 are generated 
from the NIST web database (Linstrom, 1997). All simulation run used isothermal conditions, with 
temperature set to 94<sup>o</sup>C (367.15 K). Plots of the fluid properties as function of pressure in Figure 2b shows
that the CO2 phase is super-critical.

Since the fine-scale model and CGNet have different resolutions, the saturation value used as reference 
needs to be upscaled to the coarse grid resolution. This will consequently introduce smearing to the 
reference saturation, which makes the plume outline larger than the actual one. However, we include 
plume saturation in the calculation of mismatch based on two aspects: (1) it is measurable based on 
seismicity; (2) it can help reduce the non-uniqueness of tunable parameters involved, since it has been 
observed that different initial guesses can lead to many probable combinations of parameters that give 
equally satisfactory match to the well response. In our observation, including plume saturation mismatch 
will calibrate the flow distribution in the network better, especially if the wells are sparse, as is the case in 
CO2 sequestration.

We calibrate the CGNet using the first 60 timesteps (after gas breakthrough happened), and use the 
next 40 timesteps as a testing period to see the predictive capability of the calibrated CGNet. We also 
investigated the sensitivity to different partitions and type of tuning parameters to find the optimum model

imposed on well indices and transmissibilities. Relative-permeability endpoints scalers (Swcr, Swu, Sgcr, krw
and krg) follow a fixed non-negative minimum–maximum (box) limit. To minimize the mismatch, we used 
the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm, which has proved to work well as a gradient based optimization 
method for this type of problem (Lie and Krogstad, 2022).

### Effect of Tuning Parameter Type on Training and Testing Performance

To investigate the sensitivity of tuning parameter type on training and testing performance, we compare 
two different calibration scenarios using a 25 × 25 × 1 partition: including all parameters (Case 1, 
paramSet1) and without relative-permeability scaling parameters (Case 2, paramSet2). Excluding relativepermeability endpoint scaling parameters reduces the number of tunable parameters considerably from 
4,146 to 1,516. Using the same number of optimization iterations, Case 2 gives higher mismatch for both 
the training and prediction period. Figure 5 reports the comparison of training and prediction accuracy in 
well response for the two different sets of tuning parameters.

Tuning relative-permeability parameters reduces the mismatch for the well observation in our case,

After the CGNet has been calibrated, we employ the model as a fast proxy for well schedule

$$

## Conclusions

In this work, we have demonstrated an application of coarse grid network (CGNet) models as a proxy 
of a high-resolution model for rapid simulation and optimization of CO2 sequestration with brine 
extraction. CGNet has shown to calibrate relatively robustly to observed well data and upscaled saturation 
maps. It also shows good predictive capability beyond the training period provided that the predominant 
flow regimes (i.e., two-phase flows in wells) are incorporated in the training data. Once calibrated, CGNet 
can be used for optimization by providing flow responses that are consistent with those of the fine-scale 
model. Therefore, CGNet can be a viable, physics-based proxy model alternative to a detailed reservoir 
simulation model. Another potential use of CGNet for similar scenarios would be in a full data-driven 
settings, where the model is trained directly on well observation data and plume saturation maps from 4D 
seismic, instead of simulator output.
